result:
Every year, the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther from Earth. We know this because astronauts left mirror arrays on its surface, and scientists still bounce lasers off them, timing the light's return. The measurement is precise enough to feel absurd: we can track a celestial departure down to the width of a coin.

The cause is tidal friction. Earth's rotation drags its oceans into a bulge that sits slightly ahead of the Moon, and that bulge tugs the Moon forward in its orbit while slowing our planet's spin. Days are growing longer by two thousandths of a second per century. The Moon pays for its escape with our lost momentum.

Eventually—in tens of billions of years, long after the Sun has swollen and likely consumed both—Earth would become tidally locked, one face forever turned toward its companion. Total solar eclipses are already on borrowed time; the Moon now appears slightly too small to fully cover the Sun. Someday, nothing will stand in the umbra's shadow again.

I find this strangely moving. We treat the night sky as permanent scenery, but it's an ongoing negotiation. The Moon is leaving, at the pace of fingernail growth. And yet everything we've ever known happened beneath its light: every love letter, every insomniac walk, every myth. Its departure is so slow it functions as loyalty instead of loss. Perhaps that's the kindest way anything can leave us—gradually enough to stay, in every way that matters.
